planting.note: Pot rooted cuttings or divisions in spring and grow year-round as a houseplant; the swollen caudex at the base needs excellent drainage and should never sit in standing water.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light to light shade in a fast-draining gesneriad or succulent-style mix, since this Brazilian species develops a swollen, water-storing caudex at its base. Young plants grow upright, with stems gradually arching and trailing as the plant matures, and small tubular reddish-orange flowers appear intermittently through the year above the textured, bullate green leaves. Keep the mix evenly moist during active growth but let the surface dry slightly between waterings, and avoid splashing cold water directly on the foliage. Minimum indoor temperatures should stay above 60F for steady growth.

planting.note: Grow as a compact windowsill or light-garden plant year-round; a north, east, or west window with no direct midday sun suits this hybrid well.

directions: This compact Sinningia hybrid stays under a foot tall while producing long, slender, wine-red tubular flowers almost continuously rather than in distinct flushes, making it a reliable bloomer for a small pot on a bright windowsill. Grow in a light, fast-draining gesneriad mix and keep it evenly moist, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings and avoiding cold water on the leaves. Provide bright indirect light from a north, east, or west exposure, since direct sun can scorch the foliage, and feed lightly during active growth to sustain its near-constant flowering habit.

planting.note: Train young vines onto a trellis, stake, or hanging basket rim; this vigorous species typically needs four to five feet of mature vine growth before it begins flowering.

directions: Native to the Solomon Islands, this vigorous climbing hoya produces waxy umbels of ten to twelve brilliant red flowers packed into tight two-inch clusters, with the color intensifying under brighter filtered light. Grow in a chunky, fast-draining mix and allow it to dry out between waterings, since overly wet conditions encourage root rot in the fleshy roots. Give the vine a trellis, stake, or basket to climb or cascade over, and expect several feet of vegetative growth before the first bloom cycle begins. Leave old flower spurs in place after blooming, as they reflower repeatedly over the years.

planting.note: Grow in a north- or east-facing window in a hanging basket or on a small support; stems can be allowed to cascade or trained upright.

directions: This Philippine hoya species stands out among the genus for an unusually intense, sweet fragrance released from small cream-to-white flower clusters that form along the leaf axils in fall. Its stems can be grown upright in a small pot or allowed to cascade from a hanging basket, and like most hoya it is frost-tender and grows best in a steady 65-80F range rather than being pushed to tolerate cold. Let the potting mix dry noticeably between waterings and provide bright but indirect light from a north or east window, feeding with a balanced fertilizer only while new growth is actively forming.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket where the cascading stems can trail freely; this species flowers intermittently rather than on a single predictable cycle.

directions: Native to Mexico, this Columnea species produces tubular maroon-and-yellow flowers with a bold, mottled pattern reminiscent of big-cat spots, carried along horizontally cascading stems well suited to a hanging basket. Grow in a light, humus-rich, fast-draining mix in bright indirect light, keeping the soil evenly moist without letting the pot sit waterlogged. It flowers in flushes rather than continuously and rewards fairly hands-off care once established, needing only occasional feeding during active growth and protection from temperatures below 60F. Pinch growing tips lightly after a bloom flush to keep the trailing stems full rather than sparse.

planting.note: Provide a small stake or trellis early, since this species naturally rambles rather than growing in a tidy, self-supporting habit.

directions: A Philippine native with long, narrow, prominently veined leaves, this hoya produces dense, fragrant clusters of shiny bronzy-red flowers with paler centers that rebloom repeatedly through the year once the vine is established. Its rambling, loosely climbing habit benefits from an early stake or small trellis to keep growth organized rather than sprawling. Grow in a chunky, fast-draining aroid-style mix in bright filtered light and let it dry out between waterings, since like most hoya it stores water in its leaves and resents constantly soggy roots. Minimum indoor temperatures should stay above 60F for consistent growth and flowering.

planting.note: Grow in a terrarium, cabinet, or other high-humidity enclosure for best results; this species is far less forgiving of dry household air than typical rex or cane begonias.

directions: Native to limestone rainforest understory in China, this slow-growing species begonia is collected chiefly for its extraordinary leaf texture: mature foliage develops rows of raised, cone-like bullae that give the surface a scaled, almost reptilian appearance, a texture shared with its bullate-leaf relative Begonia melanobullata. Grow in deep to partial shade in a light, humus-rich, fast-draining mix, since the thin leaves scorch quickly in any direct sun. High humidity is essential, so a closed terrarium, propagation box, or greenhouse cabinet produces far better results than open room air. Keep the mix lightly moist rather than wet, and propagate by leaf or stem cuttings taken from actively growing shoots.

planting.note: Grow in a north- or east-facing window; this Philippine species' leaves can yellow under too much direct light, so a stable bright-but-indirect exposure keeps foliage healthy green.

directions: This collector's hoya from the Philippines produces fragrant, unusually shaped flowers mainly in spring, with cooler nights and shorter day length in fall and winter often helping trigger the next bloom cycle. Its leaves can yellow as a stress response if light is too intense, so aim for bright, filtered light rather than direct sun to keep the foliage a healthy green. Grow in a chunky, fast-draining mix and let it dry out between waterings, providing a small trellis or allowing the vine to trail from a hanging basket.

planting.note: Grow on a bright windowsill or under grow lights; divide congested rosettes in spring to refresh vigor and create new plants.

directions: A boldly bicolored Cape Primrose hybrid, Kalahari carries red upper petals paired with creamy-yellow lower petals threaded with fine red veining, blooming intermittently through much of the year on a low rosette of strap-shaped leaves. Grow in bright, indirect light on a windowsill or under a light garden setup, since direct sun scorches the soft foliage while too little light suppresses flowering. Let the mix become visibly dry before watering again and avoid splashing cold water on the leaves, which can cause unsightly spotting. Feed lightly once or twice a month during active growth to sustain repeat bloom cycles.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light away from direct sun, which fades the dark pigment; increase humidity around the plant for the richest leaf color.

directions: This fibrous angel-wing-type begonia hybrid is grown for foliage that reads nearly black in low light, with velvety, textured leaves covered in fine reddish hairs and showing deep red undersides when lifted or backlit. Grow in partial shade to low, indirect light, since too much direct sun bleaches the dark pigment toward a duller bronze-green. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but never soggy, raise humidity where possible, and pinch growing tips occasionally to keep the plant full and bushy rather than leggy. Propagate easily from stem cuttings taken below a node and rooted in moist mix.

planting.note: Grow on a bright windowsill out of direct sun; divide crowded rosettes in spring to maintain vigorous, free-flowering clumps.

directions: A Japanese-bred Cape Primrose hybrid, Hototogisu sends up tall flower stems well above its rosette of strap-shaped leaves, each topped with large, heavily spotted pale purple blooms that create strong contrast against the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light in a light, well-drained mix, allowing the surface to dry visibly before the next watering and keeping cold water off the leaves to prevent spotting. Flowering is intermittent rather than constant, so a stable bright window and light monthly feeding during active growth help sustain repeat bloom flushes. Divide congested clumps every year or two to keep the plant vigorous and well shaped.
